title: GitOps
intro: GitOps principles, Argo CD, Flux and the other operators, and the tools that produce the manifests (Helm, Kustomize and alternatives). Open source and free tools only.
scope: Open source or free to use. Paid products are left out of the main groups. The Paid products group in Other tools lists a few commercial ones for awareness only.

groups.label: GitOps operators
groups.about: Agents that watch a source and keep a cluster in line with it.

groups.label: Around the operator
groups.about: Progressive delivery, promotion and image updates that sit next to Argo CD or Flux.

groups.label: Helm, Kustomize and alternatives
groups.about: Tools that turn a package or a set of patches into Kubernetes manifests.

groups.label: Secrets
groups.about: Ways to keep secrets out of Git in plain text and still deploy them with GitOps.

groups.label: Paid products
groups.about: Commercial products, listed so you know they exist, each with its closest open source alternative. Not recommendations. Details are only what the vendor's own page says.

entries.name: OpenGitOps principles
entries.summary: Four principles that define GitOps: declarative, versioned and immutable, pulled automatically, continuously reconciled.

started.basis: v1.0.0 release of the principles document

cncf.text: Overseen by the GitOps Working Group, linked to the CNCF TAG App Delivery repository. The site does not call it a CNCF working group.

sections.title: The four principles (v1.0.0)
items: Declarative: the system's desired state is expressed declaratively.
Versioned and immutable: desired state is stored so that it is immutable, versioned and keeps a complete history.
Pulled automatically: software agents automatically pull the desired state from the source.
Continuously reconciled: agents continuously observe the actual state and try to apply the desired state.

sections.title: What they mean in practice
items: Pull is the confusing one. In a push pipeline, CI applies changes to the cluster. In a pull model, an agent fetches the desired state and applies it itself. Argo CD's docs say that with automated sync, CI only has to push a commit and not call the Argo CD API.
The source is not always Git. Flux sources can be Git, OCI artifacts, Helm repositories or buckets. Argo CD's docs describe Git as the source of truth.
Reconciling means drift is corrected, not just reported. Flux reverts manual kubectl changes on the next reconcile. Argo CD only does it when selfHeal is on, and it is off by default.
A GitOps operator needs a way to render the desired state: plain YAML, Helm or Kustomize. See the Helm and Kustomize entries.

notes: The release date of v1.0.0 comes from the GitHub release, not from opengitops.dev, which shows no date.
The licence of the document is not confirmed (GitHub reports none).

entries.name: Argo CD
entries.summary: Declarative GitOps continuous delivery for Kubernetes, with a web UI, a CLI and multi-cluster support. The main subject of this topic.

started.basis: first GitHub release (v0.1.0); a press release says Intuit open sourced it in January 2018

cncf.text: Part of the Argo project. Accepted 2020-03-26 (incubating), graduated 2022-12-06.

sections.title: In one minute
items: Argo CD is a Kubernetes controller for GitOps. You describe the applications you want in Git, and Argo CD keeps comparing that desired state with the live state in the cluster.
When the two differ the application shows as `OutOfSync`, and Argo CD can sync it back, manually or automatically.
It renders Kustomize, Helm, Jsonnet, plain YAML or JSON, and custom config management plugins, then applies the result.

items.alt: You commit to Git. The repository server renders the manifests, the application controller compares them with the cluster and syncs. A Git webhook can notify the API server.
items.caption: The reconcile loop: Git is the desired state, the cluster is the live state, the controller keeps them equal.

cards.title: Application
cards.text: A source in Git (repo URL, revision, path or Helm chart) and a destination (cluster and namespace).

cards.title: Sync
cards.text: Make the cluster match Git. Manual by default, automated with `spec.syncPolicy.automated`.

cards.title: Health and drift
cards.text: Each resource shows whether it is in sync with Git and whether it is healthy.

cards.title: Project
cards.text: An AppProject groups Applications and limits which repositories, clusters and namespaces they may use.

sections.title: What you get
sections.intro: Features listed in the Argo CD docs.
items: Multi-cluster: one Argo CD can deploy to many clusters.
SSO: OIDC, OAuth2, LDAP, SAML 2.0, GitHub, GitLab, Microsoft, LinkedIn. Multi-tenancy and RBAC.
Rollback to any configuration committed in Git. Health and drift detection.
A web UI, a CLI and webhooks. Hooks around a sync. An audit trail. Prometheus metrics.

items.text: Argo CD is one application with a UI and an API server, and drift correction is opt-in (`selfHeal`). Flux is a set of controllers with custom resources, and its Kustomization reverts drift by default. See the Compare tab.
items.title: Argo CD or Flux?

sections.title: Install it (dev)

items.title: Install Argo CD in the argocd namespace

items.text: The install docs call this non-HA install "not recommended for production use". See Run it for production.

items: Lighter variants: `core-install.yaml` is headless (no API server or UI, non-HA, no multi-tenancy). `namespace-install.yaml` needs only namespace privileges and manages only the local cluster's Argo CD resources. Its CRDs are applied separately from `manifests/crds`.

sections.title: Open the UI and log in

items.title: Reach the API server and log in

items: The default certificate is self-signed: trust it, or pass `--insecure` to every CLI command.
The initial `admin` password is stored in the `argocd-initial-admin-secret` Secret. After changing the password, delete that Secret.

sections.title: Deploy your first application
sections.intro: An Application points at a path in a Git repository and at a destination cluster and namespace.

items.title: application.yaml: the guestbook example app
items.match:
name: guestbook
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default

items.title: Or create and sync it with the CLI

items: Before the first sync, `argocd app get guestbook` shows the app `OutOfSync` and its resources `Missing`.
`https://kubernetes.default.svc` is the cluster Argo CD itself runs in.

items.text: Add the `resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io` finalizer to an Application if deleting it should also delete its resources (cascading delete).
Declare apps as Application manifests in Git, even in dev, so the setup you test is the one you run in production.

sections.title: Turn on automated sync

items.title: Automated sync with prune, and with self-heal

rows: Applies Git changes without a manual step. Only `OutOfSync` applications are synced, and only once per commit SHA and parameters.
When off, resources removed from Git stay in the cluster.
When off, manual changes to live resources are not reverted.
A sync that would leave the application empty is blocked unless this is true.
`automated.enabled: false` skips automated sync even if `prune`, `selfHeal` and `allowEmpty` are set.
Failed syncs are retried with exponential backoff only if a `retry` block is set. Otherwise a failed commit is not retried.

items: Argo CD checks Git every 120 seconds plus up to 60 seconds of jitter (`timeout.reconciliation` in `argocd-cm`). A Git webhook makes it faster.

items.text: You cannot roll back an application that has automated sync enabled.

sections.title: Render with Helm or Kustomize
items: Tool detection: an explicit setting wins. Otherwise Helm if there is a `Chart.yaml`, Kustomize if there is a `kustomization.yaml`, `kustomization.yml` or `Kustomization` file, else plain YAML.

items.title: A Helm chart from a chart repository

items: Helm: Argo CD only renders the chart (`helm template`) and runs the lifecycle itself, so `helm ls` does not show its apps. The docs say it renders with Helm v4.
Value precedence: `parameters`, then `valuesObject`, then `values`, then `valueFiles`, then the chart's `values.yaml`.
Helm hooks are mapped to Argo CD hooks, not replicated: rollback and test hooks are ignored, pre-install and pre-upgrade run together, and if any Argo CD hook exists all Helm hooks are ignored.

items.title: A Kustomize patch set on the Application

items: Kustomize: fields under `spec.source.kustomize` are `namePrefix`, `nameSuffix`, `images`, `replicas`, `commonLabels`, `commonAnnotations`, `patches`, `components` and `namespace`. Several Kustomize versions can be bundled and chosen per application. Helm charts inside a kustomization need `--enable-helm` in `kustomize.buildOptions`.

Multiple sources: an Application can have several, for example a Helm chart from one repository and its values file from a Git repository referenced as `$values`. The docs say not to use it to group unrelated apps, and to reconsider past 2 or 3 sources.

items.text: A template that generates random values (some Helm functions do) keeps the app `OutOfSync`.
Source Hydrator (beta since v3.5.0, off by default): renders the manifests and commits them to a branch, which Argo CD then syncs, so the exact manifests can be reviewed in Git.

sections.title: Order a sync: hooks and waves

items.alt: A sync runs PreSync hooks, then the Sync phase wave by wave from the lowest wave, then PostSync hooks. SyncFail hooks run if the sync fails.
items.caption: Phases run in order. Inside a phase, lower waves go first, 2 seconds apart by default.

items.title: Make a resource a hook, or put it in a wave

source.label: Argo CD: sync phases and waves

items: Hooks: `PreSync`, `Sync`, `PostSync`, `SyncFail`, `Skip`, and `PreDelete` and `PostDelete` when the whole application is deleted. Set them with `argocd.argoproj.io/hook`. What each does is in Reference.
Delete policies: `HookSucceeded`, `HookFailed`, `BeforeHookCreation` (the default).
Waves: `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave` is an integer, default 0, lowest first. The order is phase, wave, kind (namespaces first), then name. Pruning runs in reverse wave order.

items.text: Hooks do not run on a selective sync.

sections.title: Manage many applications
items: App of apps: one Application whose manifests are other Applications, used for example to bootstrap a cluster.
ApplicationSet: generates Applications from a template. The template is an Application with parameter placeholders filled in by a generator.

items.alt: An ApplicationSet with a List generator produces one Application per list element, each pointing at its own cluster.
items.caption: One template, one Application per generated element.

items: The ApplicationSet controller is bundled with Argo CD since v2.3. All generators are listed in Reference.

items.text: Progressive syncs (RollingSync): beta since v3.3.0 and must be enabled. Steps select Applications by label, each step must be Healthy before the next, and `maxUpdate` limits parallel updates. It disables autosync on the generated Applications.

sections.title: Get notified
items: Triggers say when, templates say what. Subscribe with an annotation on an Application or a project: `notifications.argoproj.io/subscribe.<trigger>.<service>`. The docs show Slack, email and PagerDuty.

items.title: Subscribe an app to Slack on sync success

items.text: Put secrets in the destination cluster with an operator, so Argo CD never handles them. Named in the docs: Sealed Secrets, External Secrets Operator, Secrets Store CSI Driver, Vault Secrets Operator.
items.title: Recommended

items.text: Plugins that inject secrets while rendering (for example argocd-vault-plugin) are discouraged: the docs say Redis then caches the secrets in plaintext. Still supported, but without new features.
items.title: Discouraged

sections.title: How it is built

items.alt: Users reach the API server. The repository server fetches Git and renders manifests. The application controller compares and syncs clusters. The ApplicationSet controller creates Applications. Redis is a cache and Dex handles SSO.
items.caption: Main flows between the components (simplified). All of them run in the argocd namespace.

items: API server: gRPC and REST for the UI, the CLI and CI. Manages applications, triggers sync and rollback, stores repository and cluster credentials as Kubernetes Secrets, does authentication and RBAC, receives Git webhooks. It is stateless.
Repository server: an internal service with a local cache of the Git repositories. Given a repo URL, revision, path and template settings (for example Helm values) it returns the manifests.
Application controller: compares live and desired state, flags `OutOfSync`, can correct it, and runs the PreSync, Sync and PostSync hooks.
Redis is only a disposable cache. Dex (SSO) keeps its data in memory, so several instances can disagree.

rows: Source and destination. See Use it, step 3.
Groups applications and limits what they may use.
Labelled `argocd.argoproj.io/secret-type: repository`. A `repo-creds` Secret gives shared credentials to every repo with a matching URL prefix (longest prefix wins).
Labelled `argocd.argoproj.io/secret-type: cluster`, with `name`, `server` and a JSON `config`.
`argocd-cm`, `argocd-rbac-cm` and `argocd-cmd-params-cm`. A ConfigMap needs the label `app.kubernetes.io/part-of: argocd` or Argo CD ignores it.
`ha/install.yaml` (or `ha/namespace-install.yaml`), with a pinned version such as a release tag, not `stable`
at least three, because of pod anti-affinity rules. IPv6-only clusters are not supported
3 or more replicas, with `ARGOCD_API_SERVER_REPLICAS` set to the same number. Three also give zero-downtime upgrades
raise the StatefulSet replicas and set `ARGOCD_CONTROLLER_REPLICAS` to match, which shards the clusters across replicas
scale `argocd-repo-server` when manifest generation times out
three servers with Sentinel. Still only a cache
ingress, load balancer or Gateway, with a real certificate
items.caption: The replica, flag and setting names come from the installation, high availability, ingress and user management pages. Which combination is typical is composed from them.

items: Install `ha/install.yaml` and pin a release tag.
Expose it through an ingress, a load balancer or a Gateway. Either terminate TLS there and set `server.insecure: "true"` in `argocd-cmd-params-cm`, or pass TLS through to the API server.
Use SSO through the bundled Dex (SAML, LDAP, other connectors) or direct OIDC (`oidc.config`). Then set `admin.enabled: "false"` in `argocd-cm`.
Set RBAC in `argocd-rbac-cm`, with `policy.default` chosen deliberately.
Restrict the `default` project.
Manage Argo CD itself and its Applications from Git (app of apps or ApplicationSet).
Keep secrets out of Git (Use it, step 9).
Add a Git webhook so changes do not wait for the 120 second poll.
Take an `argocd admin export` backup before a major upgrade.

sections.title: Tuning
items: Repository server: `--parallelismlimit` caps concurrent manifest generation.
Application controller: `--status-processors` (default 20) and `--operation-processors` (default 10).
`GOMEMLIMIT` at 80 to 90 percent of the container memory limit.
Sharding algorithms for the application controller: legacy, round-robin and consistent-hashing. The last two are experimental.

sections.title: Projects and RBAC
items: An AppProject restricts source repositories, destination clusters and namespaces, which cluster-scoped kinds are allowed and which namespaced kinds are denied. It also holds roles with policies, named `proj:<project>:<role>`.

items.text: The `default` project is created automatically and allows everything. It cannot be deleted, only restricted. By default an application can also deploy to clusters outside its project: `permitOnlyProjectScopedClusters: true` prevents it.

items.title: argocd-rbac-cm: policies, groups and the default role

items: Policy: `p, <subject>, <resource>, <action>, <object>, allow|deny`. Group: `g, <user or group>, <role>`. Built-in roles: `role:readonly` and `role:admin`. An application object is `<project>/<app>`.
A deny that matches always wins. SSO group claims map to roles with `g` lines. `policy.matchMode` chooses glob or regex.

items.text: `policy.default` applies to everyone who is authenticated, and a deny cannot remove it.

sections.title: Many clusters
items: `argocd cluster add <context>` registers another cluster. It creates an `argocd-manager` service account in `kube-system`, bound to an admin-level ClusterRole.
Decide whether one Argo CD manages all clusters or each cluster runs its own. One instance shards clusters across application controller replicas.

items.text: Argo CD agent (separate project): agents on workload clusters connect to a central control plane, so the control plane does not call each cluster. The docs say 'active development with a stable core architecture'.
items.unconfirmed: A version and a maturity level for the agent are not stated.

items: Diagrams of the three models are in [Enterprise topologies: many Kubernetes clusters with GitOps](../topologies/index.html#ref-multicluster-gitops).

sections.title: Upgrades and releases
items: A new minor release about every three months (about February, May, August, November). Only the three latest minor versions get patches.
Upgrade one minor version at a time and read each guide. Major releases need a backup first.

Upgrading to 3.0 changed defaults: annotation tracking, fine-grained RBAC no longer inherited by sub-resources, logs RBAC enforced, status fields ignored in diffs, the Dex RBAC subject, repository settings only as Secrets.

sections.title: When an app stays OutOfSync
items: Common causes: controllers or mutating webhooks that change resources, fields Kubernetes drops, or Helm functions that generate random values.

items.title: Ignore a field that something else changes

items: `ignoreDifferences` on an Application, or `resource.customizations.ignoreDifferences` in `argocd-cm`, ignores fields by `jsonPointers`, `jqPathExpressions` or `managedFieldsManagers`. The sync option `RespectIgnoreDifferences=true` also honours it during sync.
Resource tracking decides which live resources belong to an app. Annotation tracking is the default since 3.0 (see Reference).

sections.title: Sync options
items: Set as an annotation on a resource or in `spec.syncPolicy.syncOptions` on the Application.

`Prune=false`, `Prune=confirm`, `Validate=false`, `SkipDryRunOnMissingResource=true`, `Delete=false`, `Delete=confirm`, `ApplyOutOfSyncOnly=true`, `PrunePropagationPolicy`, `PruneLast=true`, `Replace=true`, `Force=true`, `ServerSideApply=true`, `ClientSideApplyMigration=false`, `FailOnSharedResource=true`, `RespectIgnoreDifferences=true`, `CreateNamespace=true`.

sections.title: Hooks and delete policies

rows: after all PreSync hooks succeeded, at the same time as the manifests are applied
tells Argo CD not to apply that manifest
after all Sync hooks succeeded, the apply succeeded and all resources are Healthy
before the Application's resources are deleted. Only when the whole Application is deleted, not during a normal sync, even with pruning
after all the Application's resources are deleted
items.caption: Descriptions from the sync phases and waves page.

items: Delete policies: `HookSucceeded`, `HookFailed`, `BeforeHookCreation` (the default). Set with `argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy`.

sections.title: ApplicationSet generators
items: List, Cluster, Git, Matrix, Merge, SCM Provider, Pull Request, Cluster Decision Resource, Plugin.

rows: `app.kubernetes.io/instance`. Labels are limited to 63 characters and other tools write to the same label.

sections.title: Settings in argocd-cm
items: The docs recommend disabling the built-in tools you do not use: `kustomize.enable`, `helm.enable`, `jsonnet.enable`.
`timeout.reconciliation` sets the Git polling interval. `admin.enabled` turns the built-in admin off. `resource.customizations.ignoreDifferences` ignores fields for every app.

compare.text: Argo CD is one application with a UI and an API server, and drift correction is opt-in (selfHeal). Flux is a set of controllers with custom resources, and its Kustomization reverts drift by default.
Both deploy to many clusters. Argo CD applies from a central control plane. Fleet agents pull from a manager cluster and never get connected to from it.

notes: Origin date: the first GitHub release is 2018-03-13 and a Red Hat and Intuit press release says Intuit open sourced it in January 2018. An engineer interview says March 2018. Unconfirmed.
The docs pages show no Argo CD version. They are the stable docs read on 2026-10-26, when the latest release was v3.5.6.

Everything else is unconfirmed.

entries.name: Flux
entries.summary: A set of Kubernetes controllers (the GitOps Toolkit) that keep a cluster in line with Git, OCI, Helm or bucket sources. The closest competitor to Argo CD.

started.basis: GitHub repository of Flux v1 created; Flux v2 repository created 2020-04-24, v2.0.0 on 2023-07-05

cncf.text: Accepted 2019-07-15, incubating 2021-03-12, graduated 2022-11-30.

sections.title: Controllers and objects
items: Source controller: GitRepository, OCIRepository, HelmRepository, HelmChart, Bucket, ExternalArtifact, ArtifactGenerator. A source is checked on an interval and produces an artifact when there is a newer matching version.
Kustomize controller: Kustomization applies a path of a source, built with Kustomize.
Helm controller: HelmRelease performs a Helm release when the resource or the chart revision changes.

Notification controller: Provider, Alert, Receiver. Image reflector controller: ImageRepository, ImagePolicy. Image automation controller: ImageUpdateAutomation, which commits image updates back to Git.

Installed in the flux-system namespace by flux bootstrap, which supports GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket Server and Data Center, Gitea, Azure DevOps, AWS CodeCommit, Google Cloud Source Repositories, Oracle VBS and a generic Git server.

sections.title: Kustomization
items: Reconciles on interval (minimum 60 seconds; the concepts page says every five minutes by default). Manual kubectl changes are 'promptly reverted'. Suspend it to keep a manual change.
prune is required and removes objects deleted from the source. wait and healthChecks check health after apply. dependsOn orders Kustomizations.
postBuild.substitute and substituteFrom replace variables. decryption with provider sops decrypts SOPS-encrypted secrets, the only provider supported.
serviceAccountName makes Flux impersonate a service account, for multi-tenancy. targetNamespace, patches, images and components (experimental) work as in Kustomize.
If the path has no kustomization.yaml, Flux generates one for the manifests it finds. The docs recommend committing your own.

sections.title: HelmRelease
items: Chart from chart (a template for a HelmChart or OCIRepository) or chartRef. values and valuesFrom (ConfigMap or Secret).
install, upgrade, rollback, uninstall and test sections. Remediation strategy for upgrades is rollback or uninstall. Strategies: RemediateOnFailure (default) or RetryOnFailure.
driftDetection mode warn or enabled, with ignore rules. postRenderers take Kustomize patches and images. dependsOn orders releases.
kubeConfig deploys to a remote cluster, from a Secret or, recommended, from a ConfigMap with workload identity.

sections.title: Repository layouts
items: Monorepo (apps, infrastructure and clusters directories with Kustomize base and overlays), repo per environment, repo per team, repo per app.
Separating infrastructure from apps lets cluster add-ons reconcile first.

sections.title: Security
items: Only the Kustomize and Helm controllers are bound to cluster-admin. Tenants run through impersonated service accounts. Cross-namespace references to Secrets and ConfigMaps are blocked by default.
Images are signed with Cosign, each release has an SPDX SBOM, and from v2.0.0 the pipeline provisionally meets SLSA Build Level 3.

sections.title: Releases and history
items: A minor release at least every four months. The last three minor releases are supported. Kubernetes support is N-2 of what is supported upstream.
Flux v1 (2016) is end of life and archived. Flux v2 first release v0.0.1-alpha.1 on 2020-05-06 and v2.0.0 on 2023-07-05.
Weaveworks, the company behind Flux, shut down in early February 2024. Flux is a CNCF graduated project and kept going.

compare.text: No application controller with a UI at the centre. Everything is a custom resource and each controller can be installed on its own. SOPS decryption and image update automation are built in.

notes: Whether Flux core has a web UI is unconfirmed here. Flux Operator, a separate project, adds one.
Whether the Helm controller uses the Helm SDK, as opposed to helm template, is not confirmed by the pages read.

entries.name: Rancher Fleet
entries.summary: GitOps for fleets of clusters. A manager cluster pulls from Git and every downstream cluster agent pulls from the manager.

cncf.text: Not in the CNCF graduated or incubating list. It is a Rancher project.

sections.title: How it works
items: Deploys raw YAML, Helm charts, Kustomize or a mix from Git. Everything is converted to a Helm chart, and Helm is the deployment engine.
Two-stage pull: the controller pulls from Git (GitJob pods clone the repositories and make bundles), and each cluster agent pulls from the controller.
The controller never opens a connection to downstream clusters, so they can sit behind NAT or in private networks. Agents may be offline for a while.
Objects: GitRepo, Bundle, and BundleDeployment, the per-cluster object the agent watches and reports on.
GitRepoRestriction is deprecated in favour of Policy resources.

compare.text: Built for very many clusters, with outbound-only connections from the clusters. Argo CD has a richer UI and ApplicationSet generators.

notes: Start date is the repository creation date, not an announcement. Maintainer is read from the GitHub organisation (rancher).

entries.name: Flux v1 (legacy)
entries.summary: The original Flux, a single operator. End of life, replaced by Flux v2.

cncf.text: Superseded by Flux v2 inside the same CNCF project.

sections.title: Status
items: Flux Legacy and Helm Operator are archived. The Flux docs say development and support have stopped indefinitely and recommend migrating to v2 (migration guides exist, including from Helm Operator to the Helm controller).
The repository was archived on GitHub. The last release is 1.25.4 (2022-08-30).

notes: The exact retirement date is in a September 2022 Flux post that was not read.

entries.name: Weave GitOps
entries.summary: A UI and tooling on top of Flux from Weaveworks. The company shut down in February 2024. Treat it as inactive.

cncf.text: Not a CNCF project.

sections.title: Status

The repository says it is 'transitioning to a community driven project'.

entries.summary: Open source tool that syncs Git, OCI and Helm charts to clusters. Made by Google and linked to Google Cloud and GKE.

items: Hosted in the GoogleContainerTools GitHub organisation. The README links to a Google Cloud page and says GKE users can install it from the Cloud console or CLI.
How the open source project and the Google Cloud product relate is not explained on the page read.

entries.name: KubeVela
entries.summary: An application delivery platform. It is a CNCF incubating project, so it is listed here as a possible alternative to an Argo CD style workflow. Not a plain GitOps operator.

cncf.text: Accepted 2021-06-22, incubating.

sections.title: Notes
items: The repository describes it as 'The Modern Application Platform'.
How its GitOps support compares to Argo CD or Flux was not researched.

notes: Only the CNCF list, the repository description and the release were read.

entries.name: Flux Operator
entries.summary: A separate open source operator that installs, configures and upgrades Flux, and adds a web UI, ResourceSet and preview environments.

cncf.text: Not a CNCF project. Built by Flux core maintainers at ControlPlane.

sections.title: Notes
items: FluxInstance manages the Flux install. ResourceSet gives templated, parameterised deployments and can create environments to test pull requests. The web UI shows workloads and reconciliation.
The site also links to an enterprise distribution with separate pricing. AGPL-3.0 is a strong copyleft licence, so check it before embedding.

entries.name: Argo Rollouts
entries.summary: Blue-green and canary releases for Kubernetes. A Rollout resource replaces a Deployment.

cncf.text: Part of the Argo project, graduated 2022-12-06.

sections.title: How it works
items: A Rollout has the same spec.template as a Deployment. When it changes, the controller creates a new ReplicaSet and shifts to it following spec.strategy.
Blue-green: a preview service gets the new version, you promote it. Canary: set percentages with pauses. Analysis queries metrics (for example Prometheus, Datadog) to promote or roll back.
Traffic routers: ingress controllers (NGINX, ALB, Apache APISIX) and meshes (Istio, Linkerd, SMI).
It is a separate install from Argo CD. The docs page read does not describe how the two work together.

compare.text: The same job, the Flux side. Flagger is configured with its own custom resources and is part of the Flux family.

entries.name: Flagger
entries.summary: Progressive delivery for Kubernetes: canary, A/B and blue/green releases that shift traffic while checking metrics. Part of the Flux family.

cncf.text: The docs call it a graduated CNCF project (as part of Flux).

sections.title: How it works
items: Traffic routing: Gateway API, Istio, Linkerd, Kuma, and ingress controllers such as Contour, Gloo, NGINX, Skipper, Traefik and Apache APISIX.
Release analysis from Prometheus, InfluxDB, Datadog, New Relic, CloudWatch, Stackdriver or Graphite. Alerts to Slack, MS Teams, Discord, Rocket.
Configured with custom resources, so it fits a GitOps flow. It can be installed with Flux.

compare.text: Same purpose. Rollouts uses its own Rollout resource in place of a Deployment. Flagger belongs to the Flux family and works with Flux.

notes: How Flagger treats the Deployment it releases was not on the page read, so it is not described.

entries.name: Kargo
entries.summary: A promotion layer that works with Argo CD: moves a change from one environment to the next. Made by Akuity, from the creators of Argo.

cncf.text: Not in the CNCF graduated or incubating list.

sections.title: What it does
items: Tracks updates from Git, container images and Helm charts, and promotes container images, manifests and Helm charts through stages, with rollback.
Integrates with Argo CD to roll changes out. Its own terms (stages, freight, warehouses) were not on the page read.

notes: The licence comes from the GitHub repository, not the product page.

entries.name: Argo CD Image Updater
entries.summary: Automatic container image updates for Argo CD. It lives in argoproj-labs. Flux has this built in.

cncf.text: Hosted in argoproj-labs, not part of the graduated Argo project itself.

sections.title: Notes
items: Only the repository description was read: 'Automatic container image update for Argo CD'. How it writes back (Git or the Application) was not researched.

notes: Whether argoproj-labs projects are covered by the Argo CNCF graduation is unconfirmed.

entries.name: Helm
entries.summary: The package manager for Kubernetes. A chart is a package of templates and default values, installed as a named release that Helm tracks and can roll back.

cncf.text: Accepted 2018-06-01, graduated 2020-05-01.

version.name: Helm
version.docs: helm.sh docs (some pages not yet updated for Helm 4)

sections.title: Concepts
items: Chart: a package of Kubernetes resources. Repository: where charts are published. Release: a named installation of a chart in a cluster. Revision: the release's version number, starting at 1 and going up with each install, upgrade or rollback.
helm search hub searches Artifact Hub. helm search repo searches repositories you added.

sections.title: Typical use
items: Alone: helm install with a published chart and a values file, for software someone else maintains. Or one chart of your own with a values file per environment.

With Kustomize: patch the output of a chart that has no value for what you need. Flux HelmRelease postRenderers apply Kustomize patches after Helm renders. Kustomize's own helmCharts field needs --enable-helm and covers a subset of Helm.
With Argo CD: it renders the chart with helm template and manages the lifecycle itself, so helm list does not show its applications. With Flux: the HelmRelease performs a real Helm release.
Choose Helm for packaging, defaults, release history and rollback. Choose Kustomize to vary plain YAML between environments without templates.

sections.title: Commands
items: helm install <release> <chart> (or --generate-name), helm upgrade, helm rollback <release> <revision>, helm uninstall (--keep-history keeps the record), helm list, helm history, helm status.
helm show values, helm get values, helm create, helm lint, helm package. helm template renders locally and prints the result. See Render and upgrade flags.
--wait holds the command until pods are ready, PVCs are bound and Services have IPs, up to --timeout (default 5m0s). After the timeout the release is marked FAILED.

sections.title: Chart layout
items: Chart.yaml (required: apiVersion, name, version), values.yaml, templates/ with an optional NOTES.txt, charts/ for dependencies, crds/, values.schema.json.
apiVersion v2 is for Helm 3 and later. type is application (default) or library. Library charts only provide helpers and cannot be installed.
version is SemVer 2 and names the package. appVersion is the packaged app's version and is informational.
Since 3.3.2 unknown fields in Chart.yaml are not allowed. Custom data goes in annotations.
CRDs go in crds/. The old crd-install hook was removed in Helm 3.

sections.title: Values
items: values.yaml holds defaults. -f/--values files override them, and with several the rightmost wins. --set overrides -f. --reset-values drops earlier --set overrides on upgrade.
values.schema.json (JSON Schema) validates the final values on install, upgrade, lint and template. --skip-schema-validation turns it off.
A parent chart sets a subchart's values under the subchart's name. Subcharts cannot see parent values. global values reach every chart, but only downward.

sections.title: Templates
items: Go templates plus the Sprig library, over 60 functions. Values are read from .Values, and .Release.Name is the release name.
Pipelines: .Values.favorite.drink | repeat 5 | quote. The piped value is the last argument. quote the strings you read from values. default gives a fallback for computed values.
lookup reads live cluster objects and returns empty when nothing matches. It does not run in --dry-run, so test it with --dry-run=server.
The full function list is on Helm's Template Function List page (linked in Sources). Many of its functions come from Sprig, and Helm removes Sprig's env and expandenv on purpose.

sections.title: Built-in objects
items: Release: Name, Namespace, IsInstall, IsUpgrade, Revision (starts at 1, goes up on each upgrade or rollback), Service (always Helm).
Values: from values.yaml and the files and flags you pass. Chart: the fields of Chart.yaml, such as .Chart.Name and .Chart.Version.

Files: reads non-template files of the chart (Get, GetBytes, Glob, Lines, AsSecrets, AsConfig). Capabilities: APIVersions.Has, KubeVersion, HelmVersion. Template: Name and BasePath of the current template.

sections.title: Named templates
items: define creates a named template. It prints nothing until a template or include call renders it. Put a {{/* comment */}} above each define.
Template names are global and the last one loaded wins. Prefix the name with the chart name, for example mychart.labels. A version in the name helps between chart versions.
Files in templates/ that start with _ are not rendered as manifests. _helpers.tpl is the usual place for helpers.
A named template only sees what you pass. Call it with . to give it the top-level scope. Inside it, $ is that passed-in scope.
template is an action, so its output cannot be piped. include is a function and can be piped, as in {{- include "mychart.app" . | nindent 4 }}. The docs call include preferable.

sections.title: Flow control and whitespace
items: if / else if / else, closed by end. False is: boolean false, zero, an empty string, nil, and an empty map, slice, tuple, dict or array. Everything else is true.
with sets . to a value and skips the block when it is empty. Inside it, . cannot reach parent objects, so use $.Release.Name.
range loops over a list and sets . to each item. $ always refers to the root scope.

{{- trims whitespace on the left, -}} on the right, and newlines count as whitespace. The space after the dash matters: {{- 3 }} prints 3, {{-3 }} prints -3. indent and nindent are an alternative to managing spaces by hand.

sections.title: Common patterns
items: required fails rendering with your message when a value is empty: required "A valid foo is required!" .Values.foo. The tips page recommends it for values that must be set.
tpl evaluates a string as a template, for template strings passed in as values.
include with toYaml and nindent puts a block of YAML at the right indent: {{- include "toYaml" $value | nindent 2 }}.
Quote strings with quote, but not integers, which can break parsing in Kubernetes. Env var values are the exception and must be strings.
Roll a Deployment when a ConfigMap changes: add a checksum/config annotation using sha256sum of the ConfigMap's rendered output. This replaces the --recreate-pods flag, which is deprecated.
helm.sh/resource-policy: keep stops Helm deleting a resource on uninstall, upgrade or rollback. The resource is then orphaned.
Templates run again on every upgrade, so random output (for example a generated password) differs each time and updates the resource.

sections.title: Render and upgrade flags
items: helm template renders locally. Anything normally looked up in the cluster is faked, and server-side checks such as API support are skipped. -s/--show-only renders chosen templates, --include-crds adds CRDs, --api-versions and --kube-version set Capabilities, --set, --set-string, --set-json, --set-file and -f supply values.
--dry-run takes none, client or server. server validates against the cluster and needs connectivity.

helm upgrade --install installs when there is no release. --rollback-on-failure (formerly --atomic) rolls back on failure. --wait takes a strategy: watcher, hookOnly or legacy. A bare --wait means watcher and the default is hookOnly. --timeout applies to each Kubernetes operation, default 5m0s.

--reuse-values keeps the previous release's values and ignores new chart defaults. --reset-values uses the chart defaults. --reset-then-reuse-values resets to the new chart's defaults and then reapplies the previous release's values.

--force-replace replaces resources and --force-conflicts takes over fields in server-side apply (--force is the old name). --history-max defaults to 10. --server-side takes true, false or auto (default auto). --cleanup-on-fail deletes resources created by a failed upgrade.

sections.title: Dependencies
items: Declared in Chart.yaml with name, version and repository (URL, alias or oci://). helm dependency update fetches them into charts/.
alias includes a chart twice. condition (a YAML path to a boolean) and tags switch subcharts on or off, and condition wins. import-values copies values from child to parent.

sections.title: Hooks
items: Types: pre-install, post-install, pre-delete, post-delete, pre-upgrade, post-upgrade, pre-rollback, post-rollback, test. Set with helm.sh/hook. Order with helm.sh/hook-weight (a string, ascending, default 0).
helm.sh/hook-delete-policy: before-hook-creation (default), hook-succeeded, hook-failed. helm.sh/resource-policy: keep stops deletion.
Hook resources are not part of the release, so helm uninstall does not remove them. Job and Pod hooks block until they complete, and a failed hook fails the release. Subchart hooks always run.

sections.title: OCI registries
items: Charts can be stored in any OCI registry. helm registry login (a bare hostname only), helm push chart.tgz oci://host/path, and oci:// in pull, show, template, install and upgrade.

Install by digest (@sha256:...) is safer than by tag, because digests are immutable. A .prov file next to the .tgz is uploaded with it. The helm-sigstore plugin signs OCI charts as an alternative to GPG provenance.

sections.title: Helm 4 and support
items: Helm 4.0.0 was released on 2025-11-12 (KubeCon). Helm 3 gets bug fixes until 2026-07-08 and security fixes until 2026-11-11.

Changes: redesigned plugins (CLI, getter, post-renderer, optional WebAssembly runtime), server-side apply by default for new installs, --atomic is now --rollback-on-failure, --force is now --force-replace, kstatus-based waiting, install by OCI digest. Chart apiVersion v3 is experimental. v2 charts are unchanged.
Kubernetes skew: Helm supports the version it was built against and three before it. 4.3.x: 1.34 to 1.37. 4.2.x: 1.33 to 1.36. 4.1.x: 1.32 to 1.35. 4.0.x: 1.31 to 1.34.

sections.title: Helm with GitOps tools
items: Argo CD renders charts with helm template and runs the lifecycle itself. helm ls does not show those apps and Helm hooks are only mapped.
Flux's HelmRelease performs a Helm release, with install, upgrade, rollback and test actions.
Rancher Fleet turns everything into a Helm chart.
Kustomize can inflate a chart with helmCharts and --enable-helm, but only a subset of Helm.

compare.text: Helm templates and packages, and tracks releases in the cluster. Kustomize patches plain YAML and only renders.
Timoni is inspired by Helm and replaces templates with CUE. Module is chart, bundle is umbrella chart, instance is release.
Helmfile does not replace Helm. It lists many releases in a file and calls helm.

notes: Start date is the repository creation date. The release date for 4.0.0 is on GitHub as 2025-11-12 and in the announcement as 2025-11-12.
The registries page says it is not yet fully updated for Helm 4. Flags are read from the Helm 4.3.1 command pages. Helm 3 names (--atomic, --force) still work with a warning.
Typical use: the choice between Helm and Kustomize is common practice, not a rule stated by a page read here.

entries.name: Kustomize
entries.summary: Customizes plain, template-free Kubernetes YAML. A base holds the common resources and overlays patch it for each variant. Built into kubectl.

started.basis: GitHub repository created; built into kubectl 1.14

cncf.text: A Kubernetes sig-cli project (tracked by a KEP). Not in the CNCF graduated or incubating list.

sections.title: Idea
items: No templates and no DSL. A kustomization.yaml lists resources and changes. The original YAML stays untouched and valid on its own.

Base and overlays: the base holds the common resources, each overlay is a sibling directory with its own kustomization that refers to the base and patches it. A base can come from another repository while overlays stay in yours.

Components (since v3.7.0) hold an optional feature. They have kind Component and apiVersion kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1alpha1, and an overlay turns them on with components:. Bases and overlays use kind Kustomization, apiVersion kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1.

sections.title: Fields
items: resources: include files, directories or remote bases. components: compose kustomizations.

patches: an ordered list. Each is a strategic merge patch or a JSON6902 patch, inline or from a file. A target selects by group, version, kind, name, namespace, labelSelector or annotationSelector. name and namespace are anchored regular expressions. JSON6902 needs a target, and ~1 stands for / in a path.
images: change name, tag or digest. replicas: change a replica count. namePrefix and nameSuffix. namespace: set it on all resources.
labels and commonAnnotations add them to all resources. commonLabels is deprecated, replaced by labels.

configMapGenerator and secretGenerator build objects from literals, files or env files, and add a content hash to the name. Kustomize rewrites references to the new name, so a changed ConfigMap rolls the Deployment. Generated secrets are only base64-encoded, not encrypted.

replacements copy a field from one source into many targets (fieldPath, delimiter and index for partial replacement, create: true). openapi helps merge custom resources. sortOptions and buildMetadata also exist. generatorOptions controls generators.
helmCharts inflates a Helm chart. It needs kustomize build --enable-helm.

sections.title: kubectl and versions
items: kubectl kustomize <dir> renders. kubectl apply -k <dir> applies. Built into kubectl since 1.14.

kubectl 1.14 bundled kustomize v2.0.3 and stayed there until 1.21 moved to v4.0.5. The README lists versions up to kubectl 1.27 with v5.0.1. Run kubectl version to see what yours has. The standalone kustomize is newer than the one in kubectl.

sections.title: Limits
items: helmCharts is a subset of Helm and will only get bug fixes, security fixes and fields that match helm template flags. No private repository authentication and no post-renderer.
Custom resources may need openapi configuration for strategic merge patches, for example when the merge key is not name.
bases, vars, patchesStrategicMerge and patchesJson6902 are still listed in the field index. Whether they are deprecated is not stated there. Check the release notes before using them.

sections.title: Kustomize with GitOps tools
items: Argo CD detects it by kustomization.yaml, kustomization.yml or Kustomization. It supports namePrefix, nameSuffix, images, replicas, commonLabels, commonAnnotations, patches, components and namespace, and several Kustomize versions side by side.

Argo CD: remote bases only use the application's repository credentials. Generated resources may show OutOfSync, so use IgnoreExtraneous. Setting spec.source.kustomize.namespace is safer than spec.destination.namespace for custom resources.
Flux's Kustomization runs the Kustomize build on a path, generates a kustomization.yaml if there is none, and adds postBuild variable substitution, SOPS decryption, patches and images.

compare.text: No templates, no packaging format and no release history. You get a diff-friendly overlay of plain YAML. They combine: Flux HelmRelease postRenderers apply Kustomize patches to a Helm release.
ytt also overlays YAML but with its own templating and a data model. Carvel is a CNCF sandbox project.

notes: Start date is the repository creation date. The kubectl bundling history is from the README.
The kubernetes.io task page was cut off after secretGenerator, so images, namePrefix and overlay examples come from the Kustomize reference pages.

entries.name: Helmfile
entries.summary: A declarative file of Helm releases. It runs helm for you, so it adds a layer on top of Helm and does not replace it.

started.basis: GitHub repository created as roboll/helmfile; moved to the helmfile organisation (2022-03-27 there)

cncf.text: Not a CNCF project.

sections.title: What it does
items: helmfile.yaml describes the releases and is kept in Git. It can manage charts, Kustomizations and directories of manifests as Helm releases, and apply JSON or strategic-merge patches before install without forking upstream charts.
Needs helm and the helm-diff plugin (helmfile init installs it). It can also generate one all-in-one manifest, for use with Argo CD.
v1.0 and v1.1 are released. The maintainers say to go from v0.x straight to v1.1.

compare.text: Manages many Helm releases from one file. The same job Argo CD or Flux do in a cluster, but run from a CLI.

notes: Start date is when roboll/helmfile was created, not an announcement.

entries.name: Carvel (ytt, kapp, kapp-controller)
entries.summary: Single-purpose tools: ytt templates and overlays YAML, kapp deploys it as an app, kapp-controller is a GitOps-compatible package manager.

cncf.text: Accepted 2022-09-14, sandbox.

sections.title: Tools
items: ytt: templates and overlays Kubernetes configuration using YAML structures, not text.

kapp: installs, upgrades and deletes many resources as one application. kbld: builds or references images immutably. imgpkg: bundles configuration and images and moves them between registries. vendir: declares which files a directory holds.
kapp-controller: a GitOps-compatible package manager for continuous delivery of apps and packages. secretgen-controller: generates Secrets in-cluster and shares them between namespaces.

compare.text: Overlays and templating are separate from packaging and deploying. kapp tracks what it deployed as an app.
ytt overlays structured YAML like Kustomize patches, but adds a templating language.

notes: Start date is the ytt repository creation date. The Carvel site lists maintainers but does not say which company funds them.

entries.name: Jsonnet
entries.summary: A configuration language that extends JSON with functions and object inheritance. Output can be JSON, YAML or INI. Argo CD can render it directly.

started.basis: the site says it launched on August 6, without the year; the repository was created 2014-08-01

cncf.text: Not a CNCF project. Code owned by Google, 'not an official Google product'.

sections.title: Notes
items: Started as a 20% project in early 2014. Has a formal specification, a formatter and linter, and editor support.
Argo CD lists Jsonnet as a supported tool.

notes: The year of the August 6 launch is inferred from the repository date.

entries.name: Tanka
entries.summary: Jsonnet-based configuration utility for Kubernetes, with a diff before applying. The successor in spirit of ksonnet.

cncf.text: Not a CNCF project. Hosted in the grafana GitHub organisation.

entries.maintainer: Grafana Labs (from the GitHub organisation; the site does not say)

sections.title: Notes
items: Apps are built as reusable Jsonnet libraries. A Kubernetes library reduces boilerplate. Environments and jsonnet-bundler were not described on the page read.
The site says it is production ready and deploys Grafana Cloud.

notes: 'Successor of ksonnet' is not stated by the pages read; do not rely on it.

entries.name: ksonnet
entries.summary: An early Jsonnet-based tool for Kubernetes. Archived, do not use. Listed because it still shows up in old guides.

cncf.text: Not a CNCF project.

sections.title: Status
items: The README says work on ksonnet will end and the repositories will be archived. GitHub shows it archived on 2020-09-09.
For Jsonnet today see the Jsonnet and Tanka entries.

notes: The creator is not named on the page read (the linked post and image names point to Heptio, which VMware acquired). Unconfirmed.

entries.name: kpt
entries.summary: A package-centric toolchain to edit Kubernetes configuration with functions, built on the idea of Configuration as Data.

cncf.text: The README says kpt and the KRM Functions Catalog are a CNCF sandbox project. Not checked on the CNCF site.

sections.title: Notes
items: Parts: the kpt API (Kptfile, ResourceGroup), the CLI (package and function operations, deploy by apply or GitOps with inventory-based pruning), a function SDK and a catalog of functions.
Moved to the kptdev organisation. Why is not stated on the page read.

notes: Sandbox status is from the project's own README.

entries.name: cdk8s
entries.summary: Define Kubernetes apps in TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Java or Go. It outputs standard manifests.

started.basis: the GitHub repository dates from 2017-10-04, which looks too early for the project

cncf.text: The README says it is a CNCF sandbox project, built at AWS. Not checked on the CNCF site (the page was not found).

sections.title: Notes
items: Uses real programming languages instead of templates. The generated YAML is what Argo CD or Flux would apply.
The main repository has no release of its own. The version shown is cdk8s-core. cdk8s-cli was v2.207.70 (2026-10-21).

entries.name: Timoni
entries.summary: A package manager for Kubernetes that uses CUE instead of templates and OCI artifacts for distribution. Inspired by Helm.

cncf.text: Not a CNCF project. Created by Stefan Prodan.

sections.title: Notes
items: Apps are CUE modules, distributed as signed, semantically versioned OCI artifacts. Bundles group apps. A Bundle Runtime API handles multi-cluster delivery.
Helm mapping from the site: module is chart, bundle is umbrella chart, instance is release.
The version is below 1.0. The site makes no statement about maturity.

compare.text: Typed CUE modules instead of Go templates and values. Same release idea.

entries.name: KCL
entries.summary: A configuration and policy language with schemas and type checks. A CNCF sandbox project. Generates Kubernetes YAML.

cncf.text: Accepted 2023-09-20, sandbox.

sections.title: Notes
items: Name: Kusion Configuration Language. It was first built for the Kusion platform.
Integrations listed: Kustomize KCL plugin, Helm KCL plugin, KPT KCL SDK, kubectl KCL plugin, Crossplane KCL function. Argo CD and Flux support is not stated on the page read.

entries.name: Sealed Secrets
entries.summary: Encrypt a Secret with a public key and commit the SealedSecret. Only the controller in the cluster can decrypt it.

cncf.text: Not a CNCF project. Hosted in the bitnami GitHub organisation.

sections.title: How it works
items: A cluster-side controller and a CLI, kubeseal. kubeseal encrypts a Secret with the controller's public certificate (asymmetric). The result is a SealedSecret custom resource with spec.encryptedData.

The controller unseals it into a normal Secret that it owns, so deleting the SealedSecret deletes the Secret. The public certificate is not secret and can be saved with --fetch-cert and used offline with --cert.
Scopes: strict (default, bound to name and namespace), namespace-wide, cluster-wide.

sections.title: Keys
items: A new sealing key is created every 30 days by default (--key-renew-period, 0 disables). Old keys are kept so old SealedSecrets still decrypt. kubeseal --re-encrypt re-seals with the latest key.
Renewing the sealing key does not rotate the secret values. If a key leaks, change the secrets.
Back up the private keys (Secrets labelled sealedsecrets.bitnami.com/sealed-secrets-key). Without them, a lost cluster means lost data. kubeseal --recovery-unseal decrypts with backed-up keys.

sections.title: GitOps
items: Argo CD's secret-management docs name Sealed Secrets as a recommended in-cluster approach. Nothing else about Flux or Argo CD integration was researched.

notes: The README says only the latest version is supported for production. No maintenance notice was on the page read, and nothing was checked about Bitnami and Broadcom changes.

entries.name: External Secrets Operator
entries.summary: Reads secrets from an external store and writes them as Kubernetes Secrets. Git holds only the reference, never the value.

cncf.text: Accepted 2022-07-26, sandbox. No incubation date on the page.

entries.maintainer: Community. Started by GoDaddy; External Secrets Inc. and Pento also maintain it.

sections.title: How it works
items: ExternalSecret, SecretStore and ClusterSecretStore are the core resources. The docs navigation also lists ClusterExternalSecret, PushSecret and ClusterPushSecret.
Providers named on the page: AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Google Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, IBM Cloud Secrets Manager, CyberArk, Pulumi ESC, and many more.
Argo CD's docs name it as a recommended in-cluster approach.

notes: Refresh interval and sync details were not on the page read. The latest GitHub release is a Helm chart tag, so the version is the latest v-tag, v2.14.0.

entries.name: SOPS
entries.summary: An editor and encryptor for files in YAML, JSON, ENV, INI and binary. Commit the encrypted file and decrypt it where it is deployed.

started.basis: the site says it started at Mozilla in 2015; the repository was created 2015-08-13

cncf.text: Accepted 2023-05-17, sandbox.

entries.maintainer: A group of maintainers (it started at Mozilla)

sections.title: What it is
items: Encrypts with AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault, HuaweiCloud KMS, age and PGP. Within a major version the file format from 1.0 is kept.

How it chooses what to encrypt (values or keys) was not on the page read. The Flux guide uses an encrypted_regex of ^(data|stringData)$ in .sops.yaml creation_rules, so only those fields are encrypted.

sections.title: With Flux
items: Kustomization spec.decryption with provider sops. The private key is a Secret in flux-system: sops-age (key name ends in .agekey), sops-gpg or sops-hcvault (key name sops.vault-token).
For AWS or GCP KMS no secretRef is needed. Bind an IAM role to the kustomize-controller service account.
source-controller pulls, kustomize-controller decrypts with SOPS and applies. Do not apply the encrypted file with kubectl.
If a patch adds plaintext fields that match encrypted_regex, decryption can fail. Keep secret values in the encrypted file.

sections.title: With Argo CD
items: Not built in and not researched here. Argo CD's docs list plugins that inject secrets during rendering as the discouraged approach.

notes: Start year only: the site gives 2015 without a date.

entries.name: Secrets Store CSI Driver
entries.summary: Mounts secrets, keys and certificates from an external store into a pod as a volume, using a SecretProviderClass.

cncf.text: Not a CNCF project. Hosted in kubernetes-sigs.

entries.maintainer: Kubernetes SIGs (the page does not name the SIG)

sections.title: How it works
items: The driver is secrets-store.csi.k8s.io. A SecretProviderClass says which provider and which secrets. Pods mount them through a CSI inline volume.
Providers listed: Akeyless, AWS, Azure, Conjur, GCP, OpenBao, Vault.
Stable: several providers, SecretProviderClass, inline volume, several secret objects in one volume, Linux and Windows. Alpha: auto rotation and syncing to Kubernetes Secrets.
A patch release about monthly, and the latest two minor versions are supported.
Argo CD's docs name it as a recommended in-cluster approach.

notes: The alpha labels come from the project page and may be out of date. Not checked against the release notes.

entries.name: Argo CD Vault Plugin
entries.summary: Retrieves secrets from a secret manager and injects them into manifests while Argo CD renders them. The approach Argo CD discourages.

cncf.text: Hosted in argoproj-labs. Not a CNCF project of its own.

sections.title: Status
items: Works without an operator or CRD and can inject into Deployments and ConfigMaps as well as Secrets. Supports HashiCorp Vault, IBM Cloud Secrets Manager, AWS Secrets Manager and others.
Argo CD's docs say they strongly caution against rendering secrets. Argo CD must then read the secrets and Redis caches them in plaintext. It stays supported but gets no new features.
No deprecation notice is on the README. The last release is 2024-06-07 and the last repository push was 2024-12-18, so inactive is a judgement.

notes: Inactive is judged from the release history, not stated by the project.

entries.name: Akuity Platform
entries.summary: Commercial Argo CD service from the team behind Argo CD and Kargo. Closest open source alternative: Argo CD.

started.basis: Not stated on the vendor page read

cncf.text: Commercial product, not a CNCF project.

version.name: Akuity Platform
version.docs: vendor page, no version or date shown on it

compare.text: The open source Argo CD you run and upgrade yourself. Akuity sells the managed service.
Kargo is the open source promotion tool Akuity's promotions are built on.

notes: The Akuity Platform page itself (akuity.io/akuity-platform) was not read; the homepage names it only in navigation. Whether the service is literally managed Argo CD is not stated on the page (unconfirmed).

sections.title: What the vendor says
items: "Built by the creators of Argo CD and Kargo." It takes on "upgrades, patching, and scaling overhead".

Adds secure projects, auditability, consistent deployments across apps and clusters, one incident view of logs, events, metrics and deployment history, and approval and logging guardrails. Promotions are "built on Kargo".
A "Try it for free" button points to akuity.cloud. No prices or free tier terms are on the page.

entries.name: Harness GitOps
entries.summary: Commercial delivery platform that adds a control plane on top of Argo CD. Closest open source alternative: Argo CD.

started.basis: Not stated on the vendor page read

cncf.text: Commercial product, not a CNCF project.

version.name: Harness GitOps
version.docs: vendor page, no version or date shown on it

compare.text: Argo CD does the sync. Harness manages many Argo instances and adds governance and promotion on top.

notes: The page does not say how Harness integrates with Argo CD internally, nor whether GitOps is in the free plan (unconfirmed). The page's structured data also mentions Flux.

sections.title: What the vendor says
items: "Harness transforms Argo CD into a complete, enterprise-grade platform." It manages the health, versions and bulk operations of all Argo instances from one dashboard.
Adds a UI for ApplicationSets and rollouts, secrets from Vault or AWS referenced in manifests, OPA-based guardrails, FIPS hardened images, one audit trail and promotion across environments.
A free trial (no credit card) and a Harness Free Plan at $0 for individuals and small teams are on the page. Paid tiers and prices are not.

entries.name: Red Hat OpenShift GitOps
entries.summary: Red Hat's supported Argo CD for OpenShift, installed as an operator. Closest open source alternative: Argo CD.

started.basis: Not stated on the vendor page read

cncf.text: Commercial product, not a CNCF project.

compare.text: The same Argo CD upstream. Red Hat packages, supports and versions it for OpenShift.

notes: Relation to upstream Argo CD is inferred from the docs topics, not stated (unconfirmed). Subscription and support terms are not on the page. Version shown is the documentation release 1.22.

sections.title: What the documentation covers
items: Release 1.22 (the selector lists 1.22 down to 1.8). Topics: installing and removing the OpenShift GitOps Operator, Argo CD instances, applications and ApplicationSets, multitenancy, Argo CD Agent, Argo Rollouts, security, observability, and the argocd CLI.
The docs repeatedly refer to Argo CD, which implies it is built on it, but no page read states that, nor the bundled Argo CD version, support terms or price.

comparisons.title: Argo CD and Flux
comparisons.about: The two CNCF graduated GitOps operators.

rows.label: Shape
cells: An application with an API server, repository server and application controller. UI and CLI.
A set of controllers (source, kustomize, helm, notification, image reflector, image automation), each with custom resources.

rows.label: Sources
cells: Git is described as the source of truth.
Git, OCI, Helm repository, bucket.

rows.label: Drift
cells: selfHeal is off by default, so drift is shown as OutOfSync.
Kustomization reverts manual changes on the next reconcile. HelmRelease driftDetection is warn or enabled.

rows.label: Helm
cells: helm template, Argo CD runs the lifecycle. Helm hooks are mapped.
HelmRelease performs the Helm release, with rollback or uninstall remediation and tests.

rows.label: Kustomize
cells: Detected by file. Fields under spec.source.kustomize.
Kustomization builds a path, with postBuild substitution and patches.

rows.label: Multi-cluster
cells: Register clusters as Secrets. An agent project reverses the connection.
Per-resource kubeConfig for a remote cluster.

rows.label: Multi-tenancy
cells: AppProjects and RBAC.
Impersonated service accounts and Kubernetes RBAC.

rows.label: Secrets
cells: Put them in the cluster with an operator. Rendering them is discouraged.
SOPS decryption is built into Kustomization.

rows.label: Image updates
cells: Separate project, Argo CD Image Updater.
Built in: image reflector and automation controllers.

rows.label: Progressive delivery
cells: Argo Rollouts, Kargo for promotion.
Flagger.

rows.label: CNCF
cells: Graduated 2022-12-06.
Graduated 2022-11-30.

rows.label: Releases
cells: Minor about every 3 months, last 3 minors patched.
Minor at least every 4 months, last 3 minors supported.
